subject: Adding a third variable to ggplot

messages.author: 73d172101ebebfc8
messages.subject: Adding a third variable to ggplot
parts:
Hi all.

I'm trying to add a third variable to an empirical growth plot.
Currently I have code that samples 12 metropolitan areas from the full
data set and plots changes in a variable called "fragmentation" (FRG)
over a period of 20 years. However, I would like to add a third
variable, "segregation" (SEG), to each plot. FRG and SEG range from 0
to 1. Essentially I would like to create two lines for each variable.
Here is the code I am currently using:

id3 <- unique(met$CBSA)
n3 <- length(id)
sample3 <- sample (id,12)
plot3 <- ggplot(met[met$CBSA %in% sample3,], aes(YR, FRG, group =
CBSA)) + xlim(1987,2007) + ylim(0,1) + geom_line ()
plot3 + facet_wrap(~ CBSA, scales = "free")

Any help would be much appreciated. Thanks in advance to all who
respond!

Best,
k

messages.author: 4e69b94a09c8cf3b
messages.subject: Re: Adding a third variable to ggplot
parts:
If I have your requirement right, it sounds as though you want to use
reshape::melt (loaded with ggplot2) and get FRG and SEG as variable and
value, then plot the melt'ed result.

met.melt = melt(met, id.vars=c("FRG","SEG"))

In aes, you likely want something like aes(x=YR, y=value, group=variable)

messages.subject: Re: Adding a third variable to ggplot
parts:
Hi:

Does something like this simulate what you're looking for?

# library(ggplot2)
# Generate labels for the MSAs
levs <- paste('msa', 1:12, sep = '')

# Order levels the way you want them outputted in facet_wrap
msa <- ordered(rep(levs, each = 240), levels = levs)

# Generate a sequence of months and replicate 12 times
mon <- rep(seq(as.Date('1990-1-1'), to = as.Date('2009-12-1'),
                          by = 'month'), 12)
# Produce a data frame
d <- data.frame(msa, mon, frg = runif(2880), seg = runif(2880))
# stack frg and seg together so that we can distinguish them
# with a color aesthetic
m2 <- melt(d2, id = c('msa', 'mon'))

# generate the plot:
g <- ggplot(m2, aes(x = mon, y = value))
g + geom_path(aes(color = variable)) +
      facet_wrap( ~ msa, ncol = 2) + scale_color_discrete('Series')

# Note: geom_line() would also work in place of geom_path().

If the series are annual rather than monthly, it might help to thicken the
lines a little, as in
geom_line(aes(color = variable), size = 1)

HTH,
Dennis

messages.subject: Re: Adding a third variable to ggplot
parts:
Thanks for the responses guys. I may have failed to properly explain
what I am trying to accomplish. I'm fairly new to R so forgive me if
I'm simply misunderstanding your responses. Here is a more detailed
explanation of my data and what I am trying to graph:

I have data for 365 metropolitan areas, coded by their U.S. Census ID.
For each metro area I have annual data for segregation and
fragmentation. The description of each variable is unimportant for
these purposes, but each one ranges from 0 to 1. The data itself
ranges from 1987 to 2007. The data set is in person-period format.
Below is an abridged version of the data set.

cbsa year frg seg
1 1987 .678 .321
1 ... ... ...
1 2007 .703 .402
2 1987 .846 .555
2 ... ... ...
2 2007 .893 .560

I would like to draw a random sample of 12 of these metro areas, and
then produce 12 separate graphs, one for each metro area. I would like
each graph to include the following information:

x axis: year
y axis: generic values ranging from 0 to 1
line 1: fragmentation
line 2: segregation

I am very close to being able to do this, however I can only get one
line on each graph. Again, here is the code I am working off of:

id3 <- unique(met$CBSA)
n3 <- length(id)
sample3 <- sample (id,12)
plot3 <- ggplot(met[met$CBSA %in% sample3,], aes(YR, FRG, group =
CBSA)) + xlim(1987,2007) + ylim(0,1) + geom_line ()
plot3 + facet_wrap(~ CBSA, scales = "free")

The dataset is 'met'. 'CBSA' is the unique id for each metro area.
'YR' is the time variable, in years. 'FRG' and 'SEG' are the two
variables I am interested in. As you can see, in the above code, I
have chosen to plot FRG by YR for each of the 12 sampled metro areas.
However, I would like to add SEG to the 12 graphs as well.

I hope that helps, and again, I apologize if my limited understanding
of r code has prevented me from taking advantage of the advice given
by the previous respondents. Thanks again for all the help!

k

messages.author: 4e69b94a09c8cf3b
messages.subject: Re: Adding a third variable to ggplot
parts:
To add lines from frg and seg on the same plot, the data should be in
the same column. group works on differences in rows, not across
columns. So you want to restructure the data so that the values for frg
and seg are in the same column and a new column contains the variable
names "frg" and "seg".

The function melt does this for you. (I am using the column names from
your abridged table.)

met.melted = melt(met, id.vars=("frg","seg"))

met.melted looks something like

cbsa year variable value
1 1987 frg .678
1 1987 seg .321
...


The function melt has transformed your data from the "wide" form to the
"long" form, which is appropriate for ggplot group definition.

You will plot met.melted. The x component is still year. The y
component is now value. To separate frg from seg and plot them on the
same graph, the group is variable. The resulting aesthetic definition is

aes(year,value,group=variable)

If you are happy with your sampling, it looks as though you just need a
minor change to point to the melt'ed form. So, your plot specification
should look something like (flipping to your later variable name
specification):

plot3<- ggplot(met.melted[met.melted$CBSA %in% sample3,]) +
aes(YR, value, group = variable) + # separating out aes is
# my own weird preference

The work that you do with ggplot2 is predicated on the structure of the
data. Going from wide to long is a very common preparation step. In
addition to a great explication of the use of ggplot, the book
introduces data restructuring functions (chapter 9) available in related
packages. The book is an excellent investment.
http://tinyurl.com/ggplot2-book

Good luck!

Mark
